learningObjective: Explain the meet operator and lattice ordering choice for a canonical data-flow analysis.

canonicalClaims.claim: In classical data-flow, may-analyses use union as meet (some path suffices), must-analyses use intersection (all paths required); direction is forward for analyses reasoning about past behavior (available expressions, reaching definitions), backward for future behavior (liveness, very-busy expressions).
conditions: Lattice is a bounded semi-lattice with a defined meet operator.
The analysis converges under monotone transfer functions.
nonImplications: Does not imply meet is always union or intersection; more complex lattices (constant propagation) have richer meets.
Does not imply the direction is arbitrary; it is determined by the semantic property being tracked.

misconceptions.claim: Liveness is a must-analysis using intersection at joins.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Liveness is a may-analysis: a variable is live-in if it may be used in some future path; the meet at a block boundary is the union over successors' live-in sets.
Available expressions is a must-analysis: an expression is available at a block only if it is available on every predecessor; meet = intersection.

misconceptions.claim: The direction of a data-flow analysis is a free parameter.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Direction is determined by whether the analysis reasons about past behavior (forward) or future behavior (backward).

implementationFacts: Four-quadrant classification: forward-may (reaching defs), forward-must (available exprs), backward-may (liveness), backward-must (very-busy exprs).
Transfer functions must be monotone for the iterative algorithm to converge to a least fixpoint.
performanceScenarios: Register allocation uses liveness; CSE / GVN uses available-expressions-like reasoning.
